topic.title: Technology: Measurement and evidence in Responsible Digital Services
topic.focus: how success is evaluated and why evidence can be disputed

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Measuring the success of responsible digital services in Helsinki in Finland is harder than it looks, because the initiative was never designed with evaluation in mind. In 2018, when a four-person product team at a mid-sized software company added opt-out defaults and usage-time reminders to an app used by 300,000 people, record-keeping was not a priority, and systematic data collection began several years later. The early period is therefore documented mainly through the recollections of product designers, data-protection officers, and community moderators. These are valuable, but they cannot be checked in the way that a formal dataset can.

sections.heading: How it operates
sections.text: Current practice relies on usage logs, opt-out rates, and periodic user surveys on trust and perceived control. These records are produced as a by-product of routine audits of default settings, algorithmic recommendations, and data-collection practices ahead of each product release, rather than by a purpose-built monitoring system. The advantage is that they cost almost nothing to collect and interrupt nobody's work. The disadvantage is that people who complete trust surveys are disproportionately those already satisfied with the service, which flatters the results. Fewer than one user in twenty completes the annual trust survey. Anyone who treats these figures as precise is asking more of them than they can deliver.

sections.heading: Evidence and experience
sections.text: The strongest evidence concerns the initiative's central claim. Average daily session length fell by 22% in the year after the reminders were introduced, while monthly cancellations rose by only 3%, and both the records and the impressions of those involved agree that users report spending less time on features designed to be habit-forming and gaining more control over what data is collected about them. The evidence on costs is much weaker. Friction added to protect users also drives some of them toward less scrupulous competitors that impose no such limits, yet that effect is rarely captured by the existing measures, so it seldom appears in any summary of performance. The difference lies in how well each side is measured, not necessarily in how much each side matters.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: An independent ethics board with the power to delay a feature launch has to decide how much weight to give figures that are known to be imperfect. About 9% of users who left named the new limits as their reason for moving to a rival service. The reasons behind that figure, though, are disputed. Treating the numbers as reliable can lead to decisions that later prove mistaken. Dismissing them as worthless hands the argument to whoever speaks most persuasively. Both errors have been made at different points since 2018.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: Improving the evidence would mean paying for measurement that the initiative has so far managed without, and there is a familiar objection: exporting one market's safeguards to another without adapting them can leave users less protected than a locally designed alternative would. A smaller step would be to review the existing records for the specific weakness described above, namely that people who complete trust surveys are disproportionately those already satisfied with the service, which flatters the results. A review of that kind could be completed within a single funding year and would at least show how far the current figures can be trusted.

In 2018, when a four-person product team at a mid-sized software company added opt-out defaults and usage-time reminders to an app used by 300,000 people, record-keeping was not a priority, and systematic data collection began several years later. The early period is therefore documented mainly through the recollections of product designers, data-protection officers, and community moderators. These are valuable, but they cannot be checked in the way that a formal dataset can.

Paragraph 2 — How it operates
Current practice relies on usage logs, opt-out rates, and periodic user surveys on trust and perceived control. These records are produced as a by-product of routine audits of default settings, algorithmic recommendations, and data-collection practices ahead of each product release, rather than by a purpose-built monitoring system. The advantage is that they cost almost nothing to collect and interrupt nobody's work. The disadvantage is that people who complete trust surveys are disproportionately those already satisfied with the service, which flatters the results. Fewer than one user in twenty completes the annual trust survey. Anyone who treats these figures as precise is asking more of them than they can deliver.

Paragraph 3 — Evidence and experience
The strongest evidence concerns the initiative's central claim. Average daily session length fell by 22% in the year after the reminders were introduced, while monthly cancellations rose by only 3%, and both the records and the impressions of those involved agree that users report spending less time on features designed to be habit-forming and gaining more control over what data is collected about them. The evidence on costs is much weaker. Friction added to protect users also drives some of them toward less scrupulous competitors that impose no such limits, yet that effect is rarely captured by the existing measures, so it seldom appears in any summary of performance. The difference lies in how well each side is measured, not necessarily in how much each side matters.

Paragraph 4 — Challenges
An independent ethics board with the power to delay a feature launch has to decide how much weight to give figures that are known to be imperfect. About 9% of users who left named the new limits as their reason for moving to a rival service. The reasons behind that figure, though, are disputed. Treating the numbers as reliable can lead to decisions that later prove mistaken. Dismissing them as worthless hands the argument to whoever speaks most persuasively. Both errors have been made at different points since 2018.

Paragraph 5 — Next steps
Improving the evidence would mean paying for measurement that the initiative has so far managed without, and there is a familiar objection: exporting one market's safeguards to another without adapting them can leave users less protected than a locally designed alternative would. A smaller step would be to review the existing records for the specific weakness described above, namely that people who complete trust surveys are disproportionately those already satisfied with the service, which flatters the results.
